drafts.raw_submission: We the people demand end to end transparency for all govt. funded contracts... we need the private organizations finances as related to the government contracts... that's the end game for the only true transparency of knowing where every dollar lands.
drafts.neutral_framing: Should Clark County require end-to-end public reporting — who received the money, what it bought, and what it achieved — as a written condition of every contract, grant, and incentive the county funds?
drafts.final_wording: Should every dollar of Clark County government money — spent directly or passed through to any organization — be publicly traceable down to the receipt: who was paid, how much, and for what?
drafts.final_wording_note: Final wording chosen by the submitter on 2026-07-18, per the ownership rule. The neutral framing above was offered; the submitter chose the receipt-level version.
shaping_notes: The neutral framing converts a demand into a yes/no question an official body could actually act on, per the charter. The submitter chooses the final wording; both versions are logged per the Idea Shaper ownership rules.

Mechanism honesty: a county cannot open a private company's books. It CAN condition its own money — disclosure clauses in contracts and incentive agreements, and Arkansas courts have applied the FOIA to private entities substantially supported by public funds. The question is framed around what the county can lawfully require.

The evidence base is this corpus: $1.84M/year in EDCCC incentives with no public recipient list, commodity vendors absent from any posted record, an ambulance contract whose terms never appeared in public, and a state rebate mechanism that hides claimants. All documented, none illegal — the question is whether residents want the county to require more than the law's minimum.

Pre-vote checklist per the charter: neutrality review, human review against bright lines (no named-individual conduct — this is a policy question, clears), official partner conversation (county judge / quorum court are the actors), and conflict-of-interest disclosure: the platform's sponsor and founder is a county business owner; that relationship is disclosed on the issue page.
drafts.tier_note: Open as a Tier 0 sentiment poll during the site's quiet launch: no account, one voice per browser, changeable until close. Per the charter, Tier 0 is displayed but never cited as verified resident opinion — verification tiers arrive with the full voting layer.

requested_documents.title: The EDCCC incentive recipients and their performance terms
requested_documents.why: $1,844,538 a year in economic-development incentives, with no public list of who got it or what they promised. It sits on the money trail as a dead end.

requested_documents.title: How fire protection is funded, and the coverage map
requested_documents.why: How fire is paid for and which areas it covers — the honest basis for any fire-funding question.

requested_documents.title: The roughly $1.3 million state sales-tax rebate repayment
requested_documents.why: Local reporting says the county owes the state about $1.3M in rebate repayments — a news lead the county’s own records would confirm or correct.

requested_documents.title: The county ambulance / EMS service agreement
requested_documents.why: The terms of the county’s emergency-medical-service contract never appeared in a public document.

drafts.background: This platform traced every public dollar it could. Most of the trail is documented: the money trail cross-foots to the dollar, and what the auditors reported is quoted in full. But parts of the trail stop short of a receipt: $1.84M/year in economic development incentives with no public recipient list, commodity purchases no posted document names, and about $4M a year that moves without public detail. This question asks whether that should change — not whether anyone did anything wrong.
drafts.disclosure: This question was submitted by the platform’s founder, who owns Ozark Cleaners — the platform’s sponsor. That double relationship is disclosed here on purpose.

founding_solutions.title: Pay procurement from line-attributed accounts, so the check register publishes itself
founding_solutions.summary: Move the county’s discretionary/procurement spending onto authorized accounts tied to each budget line — virtual cards or ring-fenced accounts — whose transaction feed publishes by default. The receipt is then generated by the payment itself, not reconstructed later from records requests. This is proven infrastructure: a federal card rail (GSA SmartPay) already captures line-item transaction data at $39B+/year, one state (Oklahoma) already publishes item-level card transactions, and governments already ring-fence each line in the ledger (encumbrance accounting). Honest limit: it reaches only the ~15–30% of a budget that is operating procurement — not payroll, debt, or transfers — which is exactly where the county’s dead ends are today (the $1.84M “INCENTIVES” line). Framed as audit-and-anti-diversion, not programmable control.

citations.label: GSA SmartPay FY2025 statistics ($39.4B, ~82M transactions, Level 3 line-item data)
Oklahoma — item-level purchase-card transactions published by default
Encumbrance accounting — how governments already ring-fence each appropriation line
GAO-08-333 — the honest downside: 41–48% of purchase-card transactions failed basic controls

founding_solutions.title: Publish the county check register every month — vendor, amount, date, purpose
founding_solutions.summary: The immediately-doable version, needing no new payment rails: post every check the county writes each month, with the payee, amount, date, and purpose, in a searchable format — the way OhioCheckbook and the Texas Comptroller already do at state scale, and as Texas already sets as a local-government standard. This closes most ‘who got paid’ dead ends today, from the existing accounting system, while the deeper rails idea above is a longer project.

citations.label: OhioCheckbook — 112M state transactions online; moved Ohio from 46th to 1st in transparency
Texas Comptroller — local-government check-register transparency standard (payee, amount, date, purpose)
